name: Fatima Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, technology companies, unions or government, and this is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima Costa, 58, and I build and repair power lines for the electricity company. At the depot I check the work order, then our crew drives out with a bucket truck, harnesses and the parts list. I like being useful after a storm, though the climbing and waiting for a safe work window wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which part of the day tends to stay with you after you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A clean repair stays with me in a good way; I can point to the lights coming back on. My partner and I have grown children, but our savings are still less than a month's expenses, so a missed shift matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a better parts list could save a trip back to the depot, and that is worth something. I still want a crew member checking the pole, the weather and the actual hardware before anyone climbs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think small software changes will take away most of my field work. I do think my low pay and thin savings make every quiet week feel longer than it should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking my scheduled line shifts and ask the crew lead to show me any changed work order screen. At home I'd keep the same spending plan, because I can't save much from this pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the work itself, but uneasy about the household money. A small time saving won't make our emergency cushion suddenly large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before the crew left for a repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd match the listed insulator and connector numbers to the equipment in the truck. If the screen suggested a substitute, I'd ask the lead to confirm it was rated for that line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk with if the new list kept sending crews back for missing parts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our crew lead first and bring two examples from recent jobs. If the list is wrong, the people using it should be able to explain where it fails.

say: I welcome a quicker **parts list** when it matches the truck.
I still want a lineworker to check the **hardware** before a climb.
think: I expect small software changes to leave most of my **field work** intact.
I still worry about **low pay** and a thin household cushion.
do: Keep taking scheduled **line shifts** and ask the crew lead about screen changes.
Bring two examples of **missing parts** to the crew lead if the list fails.
feel: I feel steady about my tasks but **uneasy** about our household money.
S0.quote: I still want a crew member checking the pole, the weather and the actual hardware before anyone climbs.
fieldNote: She separates a useful **parts list** from the judgement needed at a pole.
Her confidence in the work does not remove **income pressure** at home.
She would raise a concrete work-order error with the **crew lead**.

steps.text: Keep taking scheduled electricity line shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that planning and ordering may get quicker, but a screen cannot feel a loose clamp or read a change in the wind. I would want us trained on the new process before managers judge our repair times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I see the office tasks changing first, while I still spend most of the shift outdoors. I'm junior and still learning, so I worry the company could decide it needs fewer people on each crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union representative for a practical session on the new dispatch and work-order tools. In the first year after the tools arrive, I'd practise them on real jobs and keep building my line-safety skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because fewer crew hours would hit us quickly with so little saved. Learning the tools gives me something to do, but it doesn't guarantee the company keeps my position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union representative to include in that session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for practice with dispatch changes, equipment records and the way a job gets closed out. I'd also ask who reviews an AI recommendation when the site conditions don't match the map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a new tool cut the time spent planning a repair, what would you want the crew to do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want time for a second safety check and for the newer workers to ask questions. My partner and I would need to discuss the bills if my weekly hours fell, even for a short spell.

say: I want **training** before managers use new tools to judge repair times.
I want quicker planning to leave room for **safety checks**.
think: I think office planning changes sooner than my **outdoor work**.
I fear fewer crew hours because our **savings are thin**.
do: Ask the union representative for a practical session on **dispatch tools**.
Practise the new work orders while continuing **line-safety training**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a cut in crew hours would quickly reach our bills.
S1.quote: Learning the tools gives me something to do, but it doesn't guarantee the company keeps my position.
fieldNote: She expects office planning to change before the **physical repair**.
Her **training request** is not a claim that her role is safe.
The thin cushion makes even temporary **hour cuts** consequential.

steps.text: Continue scheduled line shifts while practising new work orders
Ask the union representative for a dispatch-tools training session

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should be honest about what happens to its crews when the robots arrive. In 2028 the software could take the scheduling and records, but my work at the pole would still need people until the hands-on machines came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is hardly time to prepare at 58, and I can't assume my low-paid job lasts to retirement. I would not try to retrain for desk planning or records, because the card says AGI can do that thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union and the company for a written timeline on crew staffing and training. In 2029 I'd take any offered practice with robot safety and inspection, while keeping my regular shifts if they remain available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It frightens me because I may have only a few working years left and almost no savings to bridge a gap. I would lie awake some nights wondering whether we could cover rent if my hours disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part would you raise first when you spoke with the company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether workers would be trained to inspect robot-made repairs and what happens if a machine fails in bad weather. I'd want a real answer about pay during training, not a promise that everyone will find a new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and your partner change any plans for your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would tell our grown children we may not be able to help with large expenses for a while. That would be a hard conversation, because we have tried to be there for them even when our own cushion stayed small.

say: I want a **staffing timeline** before the machines reach our work sites.
I want to know whether robot inspection training comes with **paid time**.
think: I fear I have too little time to prepare before **2028**.
I would not retrain for desk planning that **AGI can do**.
do: Ask the union and company for a written **staffing timeline** now.
Take offered robot inspection practice in **2029** while shifts remain available.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and sometimes lose sleep over rent if my hours disappear.
S2.quote: I would lie awake some nights wondering whether we could cover rent if my hours disappeared.
fieldNote: The short runway leaves her expecting a serious risk to **household income**.
She rejects desk retraining because the scenario explicitly removes that **option**.
She names a possible sacrifice in support for her **grown children**.

steps.text: Ask the union and company for a written crew-staffing timeline
Tell the grown children the couple may pause large financial help
Take robot-safety and inspection practice in 2029 if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets the company talk with crews and plan a safer changeover. It doesn't mean my job is protected forever, since the hands-on robots follow in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That extra time matters because I could get answers before the last minute, but I'm still 58 and near retirement age. My low pay and thin savings make a long unpaid transition unrealistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd put my name down for paid robot-safety training and ask how the company will assess experienced field workers. In 2032 I'd use the first year after AGI to practise inspection tasks, while checking whether my scheduled hours remain steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than hopeless; five years gives me a little room to ask for help. I still can't count on a pension or a new job that the profile hasn't promised me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of training would be worth your time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose hands-on inspection and safe isolation around a robot, if the company pays for the hours. A course about writing schedules would be a poor bet if AGI already handles that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide the transition was no longer manageable in your current role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company cut my shifts or asked me to work beside equipment without proper instruction, I would speak with the union and my partner. Then we'd review what bills we could reduce, because there are few similar jobs nearby.

say: Five years gives the company time to plan a **safer changeover**.
I still need an honest answer about my **field job** after robots arrive.
think: I can use the warning to seek **paid safety training**.
I cannot rely on an assumed pension or **easy replacement job**.
do: Request paid robot-safety and inspection **training** now.
Check scheduled hours during **2032** and raise unsafe conditions with the union.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though the warning gives me time to ask questions.
S3.quote: A course about writing schedules would be a poor bet if AGI already handles that work.
fieldNote: She uses the five-year lead to seek a **specific paid course**.
Her plan accounts for robots arriving three years after **thinking AI**.
She refuses to treat retirement income as **guaranteed**.

steps.text: Ask the union and company for paid robot-safety training
Take paid robot-safety and inspection training if the utility offers it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives my crew and the company time to make a real plan, and that is better than a sudden order. We should still admit that robots could do much of the climbing and repair work by 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years brings me to about 68, so it may cover much of my remaining work life, but I don't know my health or retirement income that far ahead. I remain uneasy because I have less than a month's expenses saved now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for a written plan for field workers, including paid instruction and how hours might change. In 2037 I'd learn the inspection process for AI-planned repairs and decide with my partner whether I can keep working safely through the next stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to plan than in the two-year picture, but I can't make a decade of bills disappear. If my hours fall before retirement, the household would still have to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the written plan to answer first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it to say whether training hours are paid, who checks a robot's work and what happens to a worker whose post is removed. A clear answer would let us plan, even if we don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What have I not asked that I should have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask what happens to the people who trained for careful outdoor work if the machines take over the physical part too. I am proud of what I do, but pride cannot pay our bills on its own.

say: A decade gives crews time for a **real transition plan**.
The plan must face the chance that robots take over **field repairs**.
think: I would be about **68** when the robots arrive in this picture.
I cannot predict my health or household **income** that far ahead.
do: Ask for a written field-worker plan with **paid instruction** now.
Learn AI-planned repair inspection in **2037** and review work plans with my partner.
feel: I feel more prepared than in the fast scenario, but still **uneasy** about bills.
S4.quote: I am proud of what I do, but pride cannot pay our bills on its own.
fieldNote: She treats a decade as useful warning, not a **guarantee of safety**.
The age and thin savings make the remaining work years **uncertain**.
She wants transparent terms on training, oversight and **removed posts**.

steps.text: Request a written field-worker transition plan from the union and company
Keep working scheduled shifts while they remain available
Review retirement and household work plans with my partner in 2037
Learn the inspection process for AI-planned repairs in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is almost no runway before the thinking tools arrive, and robots follow in 2031. Paid training, clear staffing information and support while people move through the change would help more than being told to stay positive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a worker with low pay and very little saved is meant to bridge a gap between jobs. I want the public discussion to include our ordinary bills, not only the machines and company savings.

headlineQuote: I want the public discussion to include our ordinary bills, not only the machines and company savings.
portrait: Fatima is a **58-year-old lineworker** who takes pride in restoring power safely.
She has a partner, grown children and **thin savings**.
She expects thinking tools to change office tasks before robots reach **field repairs**.
She seeks paid training and clear staffing plans while facing **uncertain retirement income**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 leaves little warning before thinking tools arrive and robots follow in **2031**.
A job or hours loss could strain the household's **thin savings**.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid training** and written staffing information from the company and union.
She wants practical help bridging bills if workers move between **jobs**.
